extracted.intended_audience: boys and young men aspiring to be locomotive engineers; railroad apprentices, firemen, and roundhouse workers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, late-19th-century manual describing the steps, duties, habits, and technical knowledge required to progress from roundhouse helper to locomotive engineer, with operational and maintenance guidance for steam locomotives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical fitness and robust health
rubrics_metrics.description: A boy who looks forward to the honorable calling should be of robust health and perfect physically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If these conditions do not exist, he should abandon the thought at once and turn his attention to something else. Physical fitness is a precondition for success as an engineer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect lifelong hard work
rubrics_metrics.description: The boy who aims to become an engineer... must make up his mind to two things. First, that he will, all his life, have plenty of hard work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no royal road to engineering; success requires continual effort and acceptance of demanding labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin as roundhouse general helper (apprenticeship path)
rubrics_metrics.description: A position must first be obtained in the round house as general helper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with chores, cleaning, and odd jobs; this is the conventional entry path leading to oiler, fireman, and then engineer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate observation and listen to 'engine talk'
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate habits of observation, be an attentive listener and try to understand and remember the 'engine talk' that is going on about him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shrewdly pick up knowledge from watching engines being handled, repairs, and everyday work; much learning is informal and earned by attention rather than asking questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask few questions and at proper times
rubrics_metrics.description: He must not ask too many questions, and never any at improper times, unless he desires the ill-will of everybody in the yard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know when to be inquisitive; improper timing or excessive questioning will earn resentment. Observe and learn tactfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progression: oiler → fireman → engineer
rubrics_metrics.description: For a time the candidate must content himself with doing chores... By and bye he will be made an oiler, put to cleaning the big iron horse... After a time he will slip into a fireman's job, and then he must understand that his chance has come.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each stage has specific duties and learning opportunities; mastery of fireman's tasks is essential before promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make friends with and learn from your engineer
rubrics_metrics.description: Make friends with your engineer while you are acting as fireman, and learn from him all you can.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The way to make friends is to be industrious, obliging and always courteous. Good relations with an engineer increase chances of instruction and promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional conduct: no drinking, swearing, or shirking
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't drink. Don't swear. Don't lose your temper and flare out under reproof. Don't shirk your work and try to do as little as you can.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain discipline, temperance, and consistent effort; these behaviors affect reputation and promotion prospects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take pride; love the locomotive as a hobby
rubrics_metrics.description: He should love his work—the locomotive should be his hobby—and whatever contributes to enlarge his stock of information concerning it should contribute to his happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passion for the machine drives continuous self-improvement; if one cannot feel this way, he should leave the cab.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn on the engine (practical, on-the-job learning)
rubrics_metrics.description: On the engine is the only place where one can learn to be an engineer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical skills (senses, feel for the road, fire management) are acquired in service, not solely from books; every sensory impression on the engine can be a lesson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop refined sensory discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: On the engine the eye is trained to distinguish different colors at considerable distances... the ear learns to detect the slightest variation in the beats and knocks... the olfactory nerves become very sensitive so as to detect the generation of heat from friction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train vision, hearing, touch, and smell to detect early signs of mechanical or track problems; sensory skills are diagnostic tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know locomotive history and identify engines by features
rubrics_metrics.description: The model engineer should be familiar with the history of locomotive engines from Old No. 1 down to date... He will be able to say this was built by so and so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarity with makes, eras, and characteristic parts helps diagnose age, likely faults, and operational qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master coal-firing: a good fireman is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: A good fireman knows when to put on coal, how and where and just how much... unless he is a good hand at the coal shovel, he will never be a first-class engineer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Firing technique affects steam production, fuel economy, and boiler health; this knowledge must be learned while a fireman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleanliness and personal presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A model engineer is clean himself, and his engine is cleaner. Cleanliness is said to be next to godliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clean engineer and clean engine often progress faster; cleanliness correlates with professionalism and care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion on merit, not seniority
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotion according to merit should be the invariable rule on railroads. Seniority should have nothing to do with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merit-based selection ensures the best engineers run the most important trains; the text criticizes chance-based promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work by rules and principles—have reasons for actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Engine driving, to be good, must be based upon rules and principles... He who strictly observes them wins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop sound, consistently applicable rules and the rationale behind them so actions are reliable under varying conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visit special and general notice boards before duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Before going to his engine an engineer should... visit the special and general notice boards and post himself fully upon the running of the trains for the day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to read notices has caused accidents and deaths; read notices before proceeding to the engine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough inspection of engine before starting (gauge, pressure, fire, fuel, water)
rubrics_metrics.description: When on the foot plate the first thing an engineer wants to do is to inspect his engine in every part. Begin with the water in the gauge glass and ascertain its level... observe what pressure of steam there is... condition of the fire... how much coal... and that the water supply is all right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The engineer is responsible for boiler safety; a careful inspection avoids later blame and accidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspection over a pit—systematic, complete checks
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a good and a safe rule to examine an engine over a pit before starting out... The examination... should be commenced at one specified point, and continued all around the engine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect bolts, rivets, crank shaft, axle boxes, and all underframe parts; the only tools typically needed are wrenches. More engines fail from loose bolts/split pins than other causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain and monitor big ends (crank bearings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Big Ends require to be fitted brass and brass, to work well, and to be well-cottered or bolted up, but with sufficient slackness... Big End brasses do best, wear longest, and knock least, when tightened up a little at a time and often.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preventative attention and frequent small adjustments avoid overheating, knocking, and failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Little ends and bushes maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Little Ends need scarcely any supervision excepting what is required from the oiler, provided they are fitted with steel bushes. Those fitted with brasses require the same attention as Big Ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure proper lubrication and inspect depending on bush material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eccentric straps and related fittings must be secure
rubrics_metrics.description: When the eccentrics are being examined particular attention should be paid to the bolts, nuts, safety-cotters and set-pins. The bolts which hold the two halves of each eccentric strap together should always nip tightly, as any slackness always affects the engine's speed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tight, properly-cottered eccentric fittings are critical for correct valve timing and safe operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure proper condition of fire before leaving roundhouse
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no other one thing on which an engineer's good name, success and future prospects depend so much as on the condition of the fire at the beginning of the day's work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poorly-built starting fire leads to repeated trouble, increased coal consumption, and possible boiler damage; fires must be properly built and not rushed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fireman must master a set of core skills (nine-point list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before a fireman can serve on a passenger train... Here are a few things that a man must know before he can become an engineer: 1. How to make up a proper fire... 2. How to handle the shovel when the engine is running. 3. How to learn roads and signals. 4. How to calculate the effect of the weather on the rails. 5. How to manage an engine and train on varying grades. 6. How to have full control of an engine and train at full speed. 7. How to work the steam expansively and yet keep time. 8. How to regulate the water supply. 9. How to read the gauges at a glance and understand just what they mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These nine proficiencies must be learned while a fireman; they are prerequisites to being a competent engineer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Starting procedure: gentle regulator, clear water from cylinders, use sand for slipping
rubrics_metrics.description: In starting the regulator should be opened gently... Care is necessary when starting to keep the cylinders and valves clear of water... Slip or no slip, it is better to use a little sand than to incur the risk of slipping when the rails are inclined to be slippery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open regulator gradually, give a few clear puffs to rouse the fire and clear tubes, and incrementally advance the lever to avoid shock and damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnose steam blowing by listening (intermittent vs continuous)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the steam blowing? It is. Which side? ... a piston is blowing because the sound is intermittent, for the blowing through of a valve would be a continuous leaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use positional context of cranks and timing of the sound to determine which cylinder or valve is at fault; attentive listening is a diagnostic method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor 'beats' of the engine; weakening beats indicate trouble
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four beats for one revolution of the driving wheel or the crank axle... If the beats weaken--any one of them--it means trouble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn the normal rhythmic beats and never let attention be drawn from them; early detection allows easy remedy, neglect may lead to disaster.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep up steam and manage water/feeds properly
rubrics_metrics.description: To properly run your engine steam must be kept up... When the engine has got the train up to speed, steam should begin to issue from the safety valves... On long runs if the engine is not instantly up to the mark at the start... the uncertainty of ever getting the water up again becomes greater every minute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure full boiler at start, manage feed water carefully to avoid running low; withholding feeds to allow recovery is dangerous on heavy trains or in adverse weather.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and avoid bad firing (haycock cone) – build a good fire
rubrics_metrics.description: How to build a bad fire: Pile your coal up in the shape of a cone... Such a fire possesses the following characteristics: Uncertainty as regards steam making, positive certainty as regards the destruction of fire boxes and tubes... How to build a good fire: The good locomotive fire should maintain steam under all circumstances... almost resembling the inside of a saucer, shallow and concave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad (haycock) fires concentrate heat and cause damage and inefficiency; good fires are shallow, concave, consume smoke, and burn fuel to highest economy. The proper starting and maintenance of fire is essential and requires practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuality and proper timing of duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't get to your work late, and don't allow your fireman to be late. If the fire is to be properly built he has got to take time to it. Fires thrown together in a hurry always turn out bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrive on time to allow adequate preparation; rushing results in poor fires and operational problems.
